mainTopic: A son as the court's agent against his father, striking versus cursing a parent, and the laws of kidnapping
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier discussion. Cursing a father on his way to execution is punishable, just like cursing a parent after death. Then comes the final ruling: a son is never the court's agent to strike or curse his father, except when the father is a מסית. A new משנה teaches that hitting a parent is a capital crime only if it causes a חבורה, while cursing is punishable even after the parent's death. The גמרא finds the source for this in the פסוק and explains how רבי יאשיה and רבי יונתן each read the פסוקים about cursing a parent. It then shows that the תנא of the משנה compares striking to cursing, and it proves from two ברייתות about a כותי that תנאים argue about this comparison. A second משנה turns to גניבת נפש (kidnapping): when the kidnapper becomes liable, and the arguments about kidnapping one's own son or a half-slave. The גמרא discusses what counts as 'using' the victim and leaves רבי ירמיה's question unanswered (תיקו). It ends with ברייתות listing which kidnappers and victims bring liability.

steps.title: Cursing a father about to die is like cursing him after death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the earlier question: a son who curses his father on the way to execution is liable, just as one who curses a parent after death is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is just like the case of after death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers a question from just before this point: why is a son liable for cursing a father who is about to be executed? It is just like cursing a parent after death, which is also punishable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was that a father on his way to execution is treated as already dead. That does not matter for cursing, because cursing a parent is punishable even after the parent has died. So it is certainly punishable when the father is still alive, even if death is near.

keyTerms.meaning: It is just like (a comparison to a known case)
After death

phrases.english: It is just like the case of after death.
phrases.notes: Cursing a parent is punishable even after they die, so cursing a father who is about to be executed surely is too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised just before this point about cursing a father who is about to be executed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Comparison to an already-known rule (cursing after death)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A father on his way to execution counts as already dead, so cursing him should carry no penalty.
steps.terutzMaskana: Cursing carries a penalty even after death, so the son is liable here too.

steps.title: What was the final ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the final ruling was about the earlier debate: may a son act as the court's agent to punish his father?
steps.simpleTranslation: What was concluded about it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the bottom line on the earlier debate: can a son be the agent who carries out punishment on his father? This line sets up the ruling that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא brought several proofs against רב ששת's view that a son may serve as the court's agent, and none of them settled the matter. Now it asks for the final הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: What was concluded about it? (asking for the final ruling)

phrases.english: What was concluded about it?
phrases.notes: The "it" is the earlier question: may a son serve as the court's agent to strike or curse his father?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the larger debate about a son acting as an agent of the court, now that the side question is answered.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The final halacha on whether a son may be appointed to strike or curse his father.

steps.title: A son is never the agent to punish his father, except for a מסית
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא, together with a ברייתא from the school of רבי ישמעאל, rules that a son is not appointed to strike or curse his father. The one exception is a father who is a מסית, based on the פסוק "ולא תחמל ולא תכסה עליו".
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said, and the school of רבי ישמעאל taught the same: In all cases a son is not made an agent for his father to strike him or curse him. The exception is a מסית, because the Torah said: "Neither shall you spare, nor shall you conceal him."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling. A son may not be the one who carries out a beating or curse on his father, except when the father is a מסית, someone who lures people to idol worship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This settles the debate against רב ששת's view in general. The Torah's special command not to show pity to a מסית overrides the son's usual duty of respect. That is why this one case is different.

keyTerms.meaning: Agent (here, an agent of the court to carry out punishment)
One who lures others to worship idols
It was taught in the study house of רבי ישמעאל
And you shall not have pity

steps.whatToRemember: Bottom line: a son is never the court's agent to strike or curse his father, with one exception. If the father is a מסית, the Torah says not to spare him.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how strong כיבוד אב is. The son's respect for his father holds even when the father deserves punishment, and only the Torah's special command about a מסית overrides it.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said,
and so too the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:

phrases.aramaic: לַכֹּל אֵין הַבֵּן נַעֲשֶׂה שָׁלִיחַ לְאָבִיו
phrases.english: In all cases, a son is not made an agent regarding his father
to strike him or to curse him,
except for a מסית,
phrases.notes: A מסית is someone who tries to get others to worship idols.

phrases.english: for the Torah said:
"Neither shall you spare, nor shall you conceal him."
phrases.notes: דברים 13:9

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא, וְכֵן תָּנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2 with the final ruling.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A son is not appointed to strike or curse his father, except when the father is a מסית.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The halacha does not follow רב ששת's broad permission. Only a מסית father is an exception.

steps.title: Hitting a parent is punishable only if it causes a wound
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that one who hits his father or mother is liable to death only if he causes a חבורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNAH: One who strikes his father or his mother is not liable until he makes a wound on them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It says that hitting a parent is a capital crime only if the blow leaves a wound.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A blow that does not wound is forbidden, but it does not carry the death penalty. The condition of a חבורה sets the limit of the capital crime.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה (the opening of a new משנה)
One who strikes
A wound (a bruise or a blow that draws blood)
Liable (here, to the death penalty)

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who strikes his father or his mother

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה בָּהֶן חַבּוּרָה.
phrases.english: is not liable unless he makes a wound on them.
phrases.notes: "Liable" here means liable to the death penalty.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַמַּכֶּה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה בָּהֶן חַבּוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The death penalty for striking a parent requires a חבורה.

steps.title: Cursing is stricter than hitting: it applies even after death
steps.stepSummary: The משנה points out that cursing is stricter than hitting. One who curses a parent after the parent's death is liable, but one who hits a parent after death is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a stringency of cursing over striking: one who curses after death is liable, and one who strikes after death is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה compares the two crimes. It shows one way that cursing a parent is more severe than hitting one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hitting needs a חבורה, and a dead body cannot be wounded in the way that matters here. So hitting after death is exempt. Cursing has no such condition, so it stays punishable even after death.

keyTerms.meaning: A stringency (a way one law is stricter)
One who curses
Exempt

steps.whatToRemember: Hitting a parent is punishable only with a wound and only while the parent is alive. Cursing a parent is punishable even after the parent's death.

phrases.english: This is a stringency of one who curses over one who strikes:
that one who curses after death is liable,
and one who strikes after death is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה by comparing cursing with the hitting rule just stated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cursing a parent after death is punishable. Hitting a parent after death is not.

steps.title: A ברייתא learns the after-death rule from the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא. It reads the extra words "אביו ואמו קלל" as teaching that one is liable for cursing a parent even after death.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught: "He has cursed his father and his mother" teaches about after death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא that finds the source in the Torah for the משנה's rule that cursing after death is punishable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק already said "one who curses his father and his mother shall die." It then repeats "he has cursed his father and his mother." The ברייתא uses that repetition to include cursing a parent after death.

keyTerms.meaning: גמרא (start of the discussion of the משנה)
He cursed

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
"He has cursed his father and his mother" teaches about after death.
phrases.notes: ויקרא 20:9. These words repeat what the פסוק already said, so they are read as adding the after-death case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the Torah source for the משנה's rule that cursing after death is punishable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The repeated words "אביו ואמו קלל" include cursing a parent after death.

steps.title: Why the פסוק is needed: we might have compared cursing to hitting
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains why it needs a special פסוק. Without one, we might have reasoned that because hitting is punishable only while the parent is alive, cursing would be the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: For one might have thought: since the Torah made one liable for striking and made one liable for cursing, just as one who strikes is liable only while they are alive, so too one who curses is liable only while they are alive.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא shows the mistaken reasoning that the פסוק comes to block. This sets up the next part of the ברייתא, which continues after this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hitting and cursing a parent appear side by side as capital crimes, so we might link them and give cursing the same limit as hitting. Hitting only applies while the parent is alive. The extra words in the פסוק prevent us from extending that limit to cursing.

keyTerms.meaning: For one might have thought (introduces a mistaken assumption)
Since
While alive

steps.confusionAlert: This is NOT the הלכה. It is the mistaken reasoning ("one might have thought") that the פסוק comes to reject. The הלכה is that cursing is punishable even after death.

phrases.english: For one might have thought: since the Torah made one liable for striking
and made one liable for cursing,

phrases.aramaic: מָה מַכֶּה אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא מֵחַיִּים –
phrases.english: just as one who strikes is liable only while they are alive,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הַמְקַלֵּל אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא מֵחַיִּים.
phrases.english: so too one who curses is liable only while they are alive.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁיָּכוֹל, הוֹאִיל וְחִיֵּיב בַּמַּכֶּה וְחִיֵּיב בַּמְקַלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the source in step 6 is needed by showing the comparison it blocks.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without the פסוק, we would have compared cursing to hitting and limited both to a living parent.

steps.title: A second reason we might have exempted cursing after death
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds a קל וחומר from hitting to show why, without a פסוק, we would have said cursing a parent after death is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Furthermore, here is a קל וחומר. Take one who hits: the Torah treated hitting a person who is not acting like 'your people' the same as hitting one who is. Even so, hitting is not punished after death. Now take one who curses: here the Torah did not treat those two people the same. Surely cursing should also not be punished after death!
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is still building the 'we might have thought' side. It gives one more argument for exempting someone who curses a parent after death. This sets up the פסוק that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hitting is stricter in one way: it applies even to a victim who is 'not of your people.' Cursing does not get that strictness. Yet even the stricter one, hitting, has no liability after death. So the more lenient one, cursing, should surely have none either.

keyTerms.meaning: An argument from a lighter case to a heavier one (or the reverse): if the stricter case has a leniency, the lighter case surely does too
And furthermore: a second argument is being added
Literally 'not of your people': a person who does not act the way the Jewish people should act
Is it not logical? This is the standard closing line of a קל וחומר

steps.confusionAlert: This קל וחומר is NOT the final הלכה. It is the 'we might have thought' argument that the פסוק will overturn in the next step.

phrases.english: And furthermore, there is a קל וחומר:
If one who strikes, where [the Torah] treated, in his case,
one who is not 'of your people' like one who is 'of your people,'
phrases.notes: In other words, for hitting, the Torah does not care whether the victim acts properly or not.

phrases.english: yet it did not make him liable for it after death,
then one who curses, where it did not treat, in his case,
one who is not 'of your people' like one who is 'of your people,'

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ דִּין שֶׁלֹּא חִיֵּיב בּוֹ לְאַחַר מִיתָה?
phrases.english: is it not logical that it would not make him liable for it after death?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second 'we might have thought' argument to the one in step 7
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without a פסוק, a קל וחומר from hitting would exempt one who curses a parent after death

steps.title: The verse teaches liability for cursing after death
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא concludes that the extra words "אביו ואמו קלל" overturn the קל וחומר and make the curser liable even after the parent's death.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why the פסוק says, 'He has cursed his father and his mother.' This teaches liability even after death.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא closes its argument. The פסוק overrides the logic from steps 7 and 8.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Logic alone would have led us to exempt the curser. The פסוק is needed to teach the opposite. That is exactly why the Torah wrote those extra words.

keyTerms.meaning: Therefore the verse says: brings a פסוק to settle the question
After death

steps.whatToRemember: Cursing a parent is punishable even after the parent dies; hitting is not. The source is the extra phrase "אביו ואמו קלל".

phrases.english: Therefore the verse says:
'His father and his mother he has cursed': this teaches liability even after death.
phrases.notes: ויקרא 20:9

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Overturns the קל וחומר of step 8 with the פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "אביו ואמו קלל" makes one liable for cursing a parent after death

steps.title: This works for רבי יונתן, but what about רבי יאשיה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. Its reading needs the words "אביו ואמו" to be extra, which is true for רבי יונתן but not for רבי יאשיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for רבי יונתן, because for him the words 'his father and his mother' are extra. But for רבי יאשיה, what can we say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem. Not everyone has those words free to teach 'after death.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: You can only learn a new rule from words that are extra. רבי יונתן has these words free, so the ברייתא works for him. רבי יאשיה uses them for something else, so where would he learn the 'after death' rule?

keyTerms.meaning: This works well: the opening of a challenge that fits one view but not another
Is extra; left over for a new lesson
What is there to say? How would he explain it?

phrases.english: This works well according to רבי יונתן,
for whom the words 'his father and his mother' in the verse are extra.
But according to רבי יאשיה,
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the derivation in steps 6 and 9 works for every תנא
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's use of "אביו ואמו קלל" to teach liability after death
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The derivation needs extra words; for רבי יאשיה those words are already used for another lesson

steps.title: רבי יאשיה uses the verse for cursing just one parent
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא. It shows that רבי יאשיה uses "אביו ואמו קלל" to teach that cursing only one parent is enough, so the words are not free for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: Why does the verse say 'any man' (literally 'a man, a man')? To include a daughter, a טומטום, and an אנדרוגינוס. 'Who curses his father and his mother': from this I only know about cursing both. Where do I learn about cursing only his father, or only his mother? The verse says, 'His father and his mother he has cursed.' This means he cursed his father, or he cursed his mother. These are the words of רבי יאשיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source behind its challenge. It shows how רבי יאשיה reads the verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יאשיה, the first phrase alone would only cover cursing both parents together. So he needs the second phrase, "אביו ואמו קלל", to teach that one parent is enough. That uses up the words, and the challenge from step 10 stands for now.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'a man, a man'; the doubled word comes to include more people
To include
A person whose gender cannot be identified
A person with both male and female features
From where do we know?

steps.confusionAlert: This ברייתא does not answer the question from step 10. It supports the question by showing that רבי יאשיה really does use these words for something else.

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא: 'Any man (a man, a man)':
phrases.notes: ויקרא 20:9

phrases.english: Why does the verse say 'a man, a man'?
To include a daughter, a טומטום, and an אנדרוגינוס.
'Who curses his father and his mother':
from this I know only about cursing both his father and his mother.

phrases.aramaic: אָבִיו שֶׁלֹּא אִמּוֹ, אִמּוֹ שֶׁלֹּא אָבִיו – מִנַּיִין?
phrases.english: His father but not his mother, or his mother but not his father: from where do we know?
The verse says: 'His father and his mother he has cursed.'
This means he cursed his father, or he cursed his mother.
These are the words of רבי יאשיה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind the challenge in step 10
steps.raayaObject: That for רבי יאשיה the words "אביו ואמו קלל" are not extra
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where רבי יאשיה uses "אביו ואמו קלל" to make one liable for cursing just one parent

steps.title: רבי יונתן: 'and' can also mean each one alone
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן holds that a list joined by 'and' means both together and also each one alone, unless the פסוק says 'יחדיו'. So for him 'אביו ואמו קלל' is extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן says: It means both of them together, and it also means each one by itself, unless the פסוק spells out for you 'together.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives רבי יונתן's side. He does not need a special phrase to teach that cursing just one parent counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יונתן, 'his father and his mother' already includes cursing only one of them, because 'and' can mean 'or.' Only the word 'יחדיו' would limit it to both together. So the words 'אביו ואמו קלל' are free, and he can use them to teach that cursing a parent after death is punishable, as our first ברייתא said.

keyTerms.meaning: it means / it can be read as
both of them together
each one on its own
together, a word that limits the list to both at once

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the first ברייתא's reading works for רבי יונתן but not for רבי יאשיה. That difference is the point of the challenge in step 10.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yonatan says:
It means both of them together,
phrases.notes: He is talking about any list in a פסוק joined by the letter ו, like 'his father and his mother.'

phrases.english: and it also means each one by itself,
unless the verse spells out for you "together."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא quoted in step 11 by giving רבי יונתן's contrasting view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A list joined by 'and' includes each item alone unless the פסוק says 'יחדיו'. So 'אביו ואמו קלל' is extra for רבי יונתן.

steps.title: Where does רבי יאשיה learn the after-death law?
steps.stepSummary: Since רבי יאשיה already uses 'אביו ואמו קלל', the גמרא asks where he learns that cursing a parent after death is punishable.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where does he learn it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question about רבי יאשיה, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 showed that רבי יאשיה needs 'אביו ואמו קלל' to teach that cursing one parent is enough. So those words cannot also teach the after-death law for him, and he needs another source.

keyTerms.meaning: from where does he know it?

phrases.english: From where does he learn it?
phrases.notes: 'He' is רבי יאשיה, and 'it' is that cursing a parent after death is punishable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from step 11: the words are taken for רבי יאשיה, so the גמרא looks for his source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: רבי יאשיה's source for being liable for cursing a parent after death.

steps.title: He learns it from the פסוק in שמות
steps.stepSummary: רבי יאשיה learns the after-death law from the פסוק 'ומקלל אביו ואמו מות יומת'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He derives it from 'And one who curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יאשיה uses a second פסוק about cursing a parent, the one in שמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah says the law of cursing a parent twice, once in ויקרא and once in שמות. For רבי יאשיה, the main law comes from ויקרא, so the פסוק in שמות is free to teach that cursing a parent is punishable even after death.

keyTerms.meaning: he derives it
one who curses
he shall surely be put to death

phrases.english: He derives it
from "And one who curses his father or his mother shall be put to death."
phrases.notes: שמות 21:17

steps.triggerLanguage: נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מִ״וּמְקַלֵּל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ מוֹת יוּמָת״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יאשיה learns liability after death from the second פסוק, in שמות 21:17.

steps.title: What does רבי יונתן do with that פסוק?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי יונתן learns from the פסוק in שמות, since he learns the after-death law from 'אביו ואמו קלל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבי יונתן and asks what the שמות פסוק teaches him. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah has no wasted words. If רבי יונתן already has a source for the after-death law, the שמות פסוק must teach him something else.

keyTerms.meaning: and the other one (the other תנא)

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: That's רבי יונתן: what does he learn from that same פסוק?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the same question around to the other תנא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What רבי יונתן learns from the פסוק 'ומקלל אביו ואמו מות יומת'.

steps.title: It includes a daughter, a טומטום, and an אנדרוגינוס
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן uses the שמות פסוק to include a daughter, a טומטום and an אנדרוגינוס in the law of cursing a parent.
steps.simpleTranslation: That verse is needed to include a daughter, a טומטום, and an אנדרוגינוס.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that for רבי יונתן, the שמות פסוק teaches that not only a son is punished for cursing a parent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ויקרא פסוק says 'איש', a man, which could sound like only a son. The שמות פסוק says 'ומקלל', anyone who curses, so רבי יונתן uses it to include a daughter and people whose gender is unclear.

keyTerms.meaning: he needs it (for another teaching)
to include
a person whose gender cannot be seen
a person with both male and female features

phrases.english: He needs that verse
to include a daughter, a tumtum, and an androgynos.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהוּא מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְרַבּוֹת בַּת, טוּמְטוּם, וְאַנְדְּרוֹגִינוֹס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: For רבי יונתן, the שמות פסוק includes a daughter, a טומטום and an אנדרוגינוס.

steps.title: Why not learn them from 'איש איש'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יונתן does not learn those cases from the doubled words 'איש איש', the way רבי יאשיה does.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him learn it from 'איש איש'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer. There seems to be another source for including a daughter and the others, and then the שמות פסוק would be free again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא of step 11, רבי יאשיה learns a daughter, a טומטום and an אנדרוגינוס from the doubled 'איש איש'. If רבי יונתן did the same, the שמות פסוק would be extra for him, and the answer in step 16 would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: but let him derive it (from somewhere else)
'a man, a man', the doubled word in ויקרא 20:9

phrases.english: But let him derive it from "a man, a man"!
phrases.notes: ויקרא 20:9. רבי יאשיה learned exactly these cases from this doubled word in the ברייתא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יונתן needs the שמות פסוק to include a daughter, a טומטום and an אנדרוגינוס.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another source, 'איש איש', already teaches those cases (as רבי יאשיה says), so the שמות פסוק should be free for רבי יונתן.

steps.title: The Torah speaks like people speak
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן holds דברה תורה כלשון בני אדם, so the doubled 'איש איש' is just normal speech and teaches nothing extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Torah spoke in the language of people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רבי יונתן does not learn anything from the doubled word 'איש איש'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People often repeat a word when they talk ('anyone, anyone at all') without adding meaning. רבי יונתן reads 'איש איש' that way, so he needs the שמות פסוק to include a daughter and the others, and the answer of step 16 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: the Torah spoke in the normal way people speak

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יאשיה: 'איש איש' includes a daughter and the others, 'אביו ואמו קלל' teaches one parent is enough, and the שמות פסוק teaches the after-death law. רבי יונתן: 'and' already includes one parent, 'אביו ואמו קלל' teaches the after-death law, the שמות פסוק includes a daughter and the others, and 'איש איש' is just normal speech.
steps.confusionAlert: 'דברה תורה כלשון בני אדם' does not mean the Torah has wasted words in general. Here it means only that this particular doubling is a normal way of speaking, so no extra law is learned from it.

phrases.english: The Torah spoke
in the language of people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A difference in how the two תנאים read the Torah: רבי יונתן does not learn from doubled words.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רבי יונתן could learn a daughter and the others from 'איש איש', which would make the שמות פסוק extra.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי יונתן, 'איש איש' is ordinary speech, so the שמות פסוק is needed to include a daughter, a טומטום and an אנדרוגינוס.

steps.title: Why not list another way striking is stricter than cursing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה did not also teach that striking a parent is stricter than cursing, since striking is forbidden even toward a parent who does not act like 'your people.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the משנה also teach: striking is stricter than cursing, because with striking the Torah treated someone who does not act like 'your people' the same as someone who does, and that is not so with cursing.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה listed one way cursing a parent is stricter than striking. The גמרא asks why it didn't also list a way that striking is stricter than cursing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For cursing, the rule only protects someone who acts like 'your people' (עושה מעשה עמך), so cursing a sinful parent is not punished the same way. For striking, the Torah forbids it even when the parent is a sinner. So striking has its own stringency, and the גמרא asks why the משנה left it out.

keyTerms.meaning: a stringency; a way one law is stricter than another
one who strikes (here, his parent)
one who curses (here, his parent)
'among your people', someone who acts as a proper member of the Jewish people

phrases.english: And let it teach: a stringency in one who strikes over one who curses,
that with one who strikes, [the Torah] made with him
one not of your people like one of your people,
phrases.notes: 'Not of your people' means a parent who is a sinner and does not act like a proper Jew.

phrases.english: which is not so with one who curses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the wording of the משנה after the side discussion of רבי יאשיה and רבי יונתן.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's list of stringencies between cursing and striking a parent.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If striking also has a stringency over cursing (it applies even to a sinful parent), the משנה should have mentioned it too.

steps.title: The משנה compares striking to cursing
steps.stepSummary: The תנא of the משנה holds that striking is compared to cursing, so the sinner rule is the same for both and there is no extra stringency to list.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds that we compare striking to cursing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the תנא of the משנה treats striking and cursing the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If הכאה is compared to קללה, then just as cursing a sinful parent is not punished, striking a sinful parent is not punished either. That means the difference from step 19 does not exist for this תנא, so he had nothing to add.

keyTerms.meaning: he holds
we compare (two laws to each other because the Torah places them side by side)
striking
cursing

phrases.english: He holds: we compare striking to cursing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The תנא holds a different underlying rule, which removes the supposed difference.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Striking is forbidden even toward a sinner, unlike cursing, so the משנה should list it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תנא of the משנה compares הכאה to קללה, so both have the same rule about a sinner and there is no extra stringency.
steps.whyThisMatters: This idea of comparing הכאה to קללה becomes the topic the rest of this section tests.

steps.title: Two ברייתות about striking and cursing a כותי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the same question is argued in two ברייתות. One says you may not strike a כותי but may curse him. The other says you may do neither.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say these תנאים argue like those תנאים? One ברייתא teaches: a כותי, you are commanded about striking him but not about cursing him. Another ברייתא teaches: you are commanded neither about cursing him nor about striking him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a suggestion that the question 'do we compare striking to cursing?' is already argued in two ברייתות. Here it quotes the two ברייתות. The next step will explain the link.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא treats striking and cursing a כותי differently. The second treats them the same, saying neither is forbidden. That difference looks like it could match the question of whether הכאה is compared to קללה.

keyTerms.meaning: shall we say? (opens a suggestion that may be rejected)
these תנאים argue like those תנאים, meaning the two arguments are really the same argument
a Samaritan, from the people brought into ארץ ישראל who converted
commanded (here, commanded not to do it)

phrases.english: Shall we say: these תנאים are like those תנאים?
For one [ברייתא] teaches: a כותי:
you are commanded about striking him,
phrases.notes: Meaning you are commanded not to strike him.

phrases.english: but you are not commanded about cursing him.
And another [ברייתא] teaches:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה לֹא עַל קִלְלָתוֹ וְלֹא עַל הַכָּאָתוֹ.
phrases.english: you are commanded neither about cursing him nor about striking him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the rule from step 20 (comparing הכאה to קללה) and looks for an older argument about it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the question of comparing הכאה to קללה the same as the argument between the two ברייתות about a כותי?

steps.title: The suggested reason the ברייתות argue
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא assumes both ברייתות agree כותים are true converts, so their argument must be about whether striking is compared to cursing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They assumed that everyone agrees כותים are true converts. Isn't it that they argue about this: one holds we compare striking to cursing, and one holds we do not compare striking to cursing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the two ברייתות seem to argue about comparing striking to cursing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If כותים are true converts, a כותי who sins is like a Jew who sins. You may curse such a sinner, since he is not acting like 'your people.' The ברייתא that forbids striking him does not compare striking to cursing. The ברייתא that allows both does compare them.

keyTerms.meaning: they assumed (the גמרא's starting assumption)
everyone (both sides agree)
true converts
isn't it that...? (introduces a proposed proof)
they argue

phrases.english: They assumed that everyone [agrees]
כותים are true converts.
Isn't it that they argue about this?
That one master holds: we compare striking to cursing,
phrases.notes: This is the second ברייתא: both are allowed against a sinner.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: לָא מַקְּשִׁינַן הַכָּאָה לִקְלָלָה.
phrases.english: and one master holds: we do not compare striking to cursing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the suggestion opened in step 21 by explaining the link.
steps.raayaObject: That comparing הכאה to קללה is argued among תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The two ברייתות about striking and cursing a כותי, if we assume both see כותים as true converts.

steps.title: They really argue about whether כותים are true converts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Both ברייתות agree we do not compare striking to cursing. They argue whether כותים are true converts or converted only out of fear of lions.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees we do not compare striking to cursing. Here they argue about this: one holds כותים are true converts, and one holds כותים are 'lion converts.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back and gives a different reason for the argument between the ברייתות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If כותים are true converts, a sinning כותי is like a sinning Jew: you may curse him but not strike him (first ברייתא). If they converted only out of fear of lions, the conversion never counted. They are treated like non-Jews, so neither rule protects them (second ברייתא). So the ברייתות do not show any argument about comparing הכאה to קללה.

keyTerms.meaning: no (opens a rejection)
and here (in this case)
'lion converts', who converted out of fear of lions, so the conversion is not real

steps.whatToRemember: The two ברייתות about a כותי do not prove an argument over comparing הכאה to קללה. Both can hold we don't compare them; they argue whether כותים are גירי אמת or גירי אריות.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two ways of reading the ברייתות: first the גמרא assumed everyone agrees on כותים and they argue about comparing; in the end, everyone agrees on not comparing and they argue about כותים.

phrases.english: No, everyone [agrees]
we do not compare striking to cursing,
and here they argue about this:

phrases.aramaic: מָר סָבַר כּוּתִים גֵּירֵי אֱמֶת הֵן,
phrases.english: one master holds כותים are true converts,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר כּוּתִים גֵּירֵי אֲרָיוֹת הֵן.
phrases.english: and one master holds כותים are lion converts.
phrases.notes: This refers to the lions sent among them in מלכים ב פרק 17, which pushed them to convert out of fear.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא מַקְּשִׁינַן הַכָּאָה לִקְלָלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof suggested in steps 21 and 22.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the claim that the ברייתות argue about comparing הכאה to קללה. The ברייתות themselves stand.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The starting assumption that everyone agrees כותים are true converts is wrong. The real argument is about the status of כותים.

steps.title: The second ברייתא treats a כותי's ox like a Jew's ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the last rejection. The second ברייתא also says a כותי's ox is like a Jew's ox, which shows it sees כותים as full converts.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, how does that fit with what is taught in that same ברייתא: 'and his ox is like a Jew's'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 23. That answer said the second ברייתא sees כותים as converts only out of fear of lions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second ברייתא says a כותי's ox is treated like a Jewish person's ox for damages. That only makes sense if the ברייתא treats כותים as full Jews. So it cannot hold that they converted only out of fear, and the rejection in step 23 falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: introduces a problem with what was just said
Is that what is taught about it? A sarcastic 'how does that fit?'
His ox

phrases.english: If so,
does that fit with what is taught about it:
"And his ox is like a Jew's"?
phrases.notes: This is another line in the second ברייתא, the one that says you are not commanded about either striking or cursing a כותי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in step 23 by quoting more of the second ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the second ברייתא sees כותים as converts only out of fear of lions
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second ברייתא gives a כותי's ox the full status of a Jew's ox, which only works if it treats כותים as full converts.

steps.title: Conclusion: the ברייתות argue about comparing striking to cursing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to its first suggestion. The two ברייתות really argue about whether striking is compared to cursing, and the גמרא confirms it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, learn from this that they argue about the comparison. Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the rejection and goes back to the suggestion from steps 21-22. It closes the topic with 'שמע מינה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ברייתות agree that כותים are full converts. So the only way to explain their argument is the היקש. One ברייתא does not compare striking to cursing, so striking a כותי is forbidden but cursing is allowed. The other does compare them, so neither is forbidden: just as cursing a sinner is allowed, striking him is allowed too.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it; conclude from it
The comparison (היקש) between striking and cursing
They disagree

steps.whatToRemember: The final answer: the two ברייתות about a כותי argue about whether striking is compared to cursing, not about whether כותים are real converts.

phrases.english: Rather, learn from it:
they disagree about the comparison.
phrases.notes: He means the comparison between striking and cursing from steps 20-22.

phrases.english: Conclude from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: בְּהֶיקֵּישָׁא פְּלִיגִי. שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the challenge in step 24 and brings back the suggestion of step 22.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The two ברייתות argue about whether striking is compared to cursing.

steps.title: New משנה: when a kidnapper becomes liable
steps.stepSummary: A kidnapper is liable only once he brings the victim into his domain. רבי יהודה says he must also use the victim, based on the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who kidnaps a Jew is not liable until he brings him into his domain. רבי יהודה says: until he brings him into his domain and uses him, as it says: 'and he exploited him and sold him.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins about גניבת נפש, kidnapping a person. It gives the conditions for the death penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees the victim must be taken into the kidnapper's domain. רבי יהודה adds a second condition: the kidnapper must also make use of the victim. He learns this from the word 'והתעמר' in the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: One who kidnaps a person
That he brings him into his own domain
And he exploited him (used him)
And he uses him

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who kidnaps a Jewish person
is not liable until he brings him into his domain.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
until he brings him into his domain and uses him,
as it is said:
"and he exploited him and sold him."
phrases.notes: דברים 24:7

steps.triggerLanguage: הַגּוֹנֵב נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיַּכְנִיסֶנּוּ לִרְשׁוּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic, kidnapping.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A kidnapper is liable only after bringing the victim into his domain. רבי יהודה also requires that he use the victim.

steps.title: Kidnapping one's own son
steps.stepSummary: If a man kidnaps his own son, רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה says he is liable, and the חכמים say he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who kidnaps his own son: רבי ישמעאל the son of רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה holds him liable, and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a second case: a father who kidnaps his own son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives no reasons here. It only records that one תנא holds the father liable and the חכמים exempt him.

keyTerms.meaning: One who kidnaps his own son
Holds him liable
Exempt him

phrases.english: One who kidnaps his own son,

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה מְחַיֵּיב,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka, holds him liable,
and the Rabbis exempt him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second case to the kidnapping משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute over whether a father who kidnaps his son is liable.

steps.title: Kidnapping a half-slave, half-free person
steps.stepSummary: If someone kidnaps a person who is half slave and half free, רבי יהודה holds him liable and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he kidnapped someone who is half slave and half free, רבי יהודה holds him liable, and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends with a third case: kidnapping a person who is partly a slave and partly free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether a person with mixed status counts as the kind of victim the Torah means. רבי יהודה says the kidnapper is liable. The חכמים say he is not.

keyTerms.meaning: Half slave and half free

phrases.aramaic: גָּנַב מִי שֶׁחֶצְיוֹ עֶבֶד וְחֶצְיוֹ בֶּן חוֹרִין,
phrases.english: If he kidnapped one who is half slave and half free,
Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable,
and the Rabbis exempt him.

steps.triggerLanguage: גָּנַב מִי שֶׁחֶצְיוֹ עֶבֶד וְחֶצְיוֹ בֶּן חוֹרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the third and last case of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute over kidnapping a half-slave, half-free person.

steps.title: Does the first תנא really not need 'using'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the תנא קמא could leave out the requirement of using the victim, since the פסוק says 'והתעמר בו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And does the first תנא not require using the victim?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts on the משנה. It asks about the first opinion, which seems to ignore an explicit word in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא only mentioned bringing the victim into the kidnapper's domain. But the Torah clearly says 'והתעמר בו', and no one would simply ignore a word in the פסוק. So there must be a different point the two opinions argue about.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed opinion in the משנה
Exploiting or using the victim
Does not require

phrases.english: GEMARA: And the first tanna,
does he not require exploitation?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the first part of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The opinion of the תנא קמא in the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק says 'והתעמר בו', so every opinion should need some kind of use.

steps.title: They argue about use worth less than a פרוטה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אחא בריה דרבא answers that everyone needs use. The argument is about use worth less than a פרוטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אחא the son of רבא said: The difference between them is use worth less than a פרוטה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 29. Both opinions agree that some use is needed, and the argument is only about very small use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the תנא קמא, any use at all is enough, even use worth less than a פרוטה. That is why he did not bother to mention it. רבי יהודה requires use worth at least a פרוטה.

keyTerms.meaning: Less than the value of a פרוטה, the smallest coin
There is a difference between them

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the תנא קמא does not need use at all. He needs it too. He just accepts even a tiny amount.

phrases.english: Rabbi Aḥa, son of Rava, said:
exploitation worth less than a peruta
is the difference between them.

steps.triggerLanguage: עִימּוּר פָּחוֹת מִשָּׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the dispute to a narrower point (the amount of use)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תנא קמא seemed to require no use at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both require use. The תנא קמא accepts any amount, while רבי יהודה requires at least a פרוטה's worth.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה asks: is this a kind of 'using'?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks about two cases: selling a kidnapped person while he is asleep, and selling a pregnant woman for her unborn child. Does either count as 'using'?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked: If he kidnapped someone and sold him while he was asleep, what is the law? If he sold a woman for her unborn child, what is the law? Is that a kind of using, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה raises a question about the limits of עימור, the 'using' the פסוק requires.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases the kidnapper did not get normal work out of the victim. A sleeping person does nothing, and a woman sold for her unborn child is valued for the baby, not for her own labor. The question is whether these still count as the 'using' that makes a kidnapper liable.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked a question that has no clear answer yet
Asleep
For her unborn child
A way of using or exploiting

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked:
If he kidnapped him and sold him while asleep, what is the law?
If he sold a woman for her fetus, what is the law?
phrases.notes: He means a pregnant woman who was sold only for the value of her unborn baby.

phrases.english: Is this a way of exploitation,
or is this not a way of exploitation?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the requirement of עימור and tests its limits with unusual cases.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether selling a sleeping person, or selling a pregnant woman for her fetus, counts as עימור for liability.

steps.title: There is no using at all here
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי ירמיה's questions: a sleeping person or an unborn baby is not being used at all, so the answer should be obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why ask? There is no using at all, so he should simply be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי ירמיה's questions from the step before. If nothing is done with the victim, why is this even a question?
steps.deeperAnalysis: We learned that the kidnapper needs עימור (using the victim) to be liable. Selling a sleeping person, or a woman for her unborn child, seems to involve no using at all. So he should clearly be exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him just conclude it from a simpler reason
Using or making use of the kidnapped person
There is not

phrases.english: But let him derive it
phrases.notes: This goes back to רבי ירמיה's two questions from the step before.

phrases.english: since there is no using at all?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רבי ירמיה's question was a real question at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ירמיה's questions about a sleeper and a pregnant woman
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Use of the victim is required. In these cases there is no use at all, so the kidnapper is clearly exempt and there is nothing to ask.

steps.title: The question is about leaning on a sleeper or using a woman to block the wind
steps.stepSummary: The question is needed only when he leaned on the sleeping person, or stood the pregnant woman in front of the wind. Is that a kind of using?
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for a case where he leaned on the sleeper, or stood the woman up to block the wind. Does that count as using him, or not? What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רבי ירמיה was asking about cases with some small use of the victim. Then it asks whether that kind of use counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaning on someone or using a person as a windbreak is a real benefit, but it is an unusual kind of use. The question is whether this is the normal way of 'using' a person that the פסוק means.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for a specific case
He leaned or reclined on him
In front of the wind
A normal way of using

phrases.english: No, it is needed
a sleeping person — where he leaned on him
a woman — where he stood her in front of the wind
phrases.notes: He used her body to shield himself from the wind.

phrases.english: Is this a way of using
or is this not a way of using?
What is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by narrowing the cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The questions were about cases with no use at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: The questions are about cases with an unusual kind of use, such as leaning on someone or using them as a windbreak.

steps.title: The question stays unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends with תיקו. The question is left open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot answer the question, so it leaves it unresolved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source decides whether leaning on someone or using someone as a windbreak counts as 'using.' The question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question remains unanswered

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question with no answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether an unusual use like leaning on a sleeper or using a woman as a windbreak counts as עימור stays unresolved.

steps.title: A woman who kidnaps is also liable
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: the פסוק in דברים says 'a man,' but the פסוק in שמות includes a woman kidnapper too.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'If a man is found kidnapping a person from his brothers.' This only teaches about a man who kidnaps. How do we know a woman is liable too? The פסוק says: 'And one who kidnaps a man.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a ברייתא showing that a woman who kidnaps is liable just like a man.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in דברים says 'איש,' a man, is the kidnapper. The פסוק in שמות, 'וגונב איש,' does not say whether the kidnapper is male or female. So it includes a woman kidnapper.

keyTerms.meaning: I only know this much
From where do we know?
The פסוק teaches

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
'If a man is found
kidnapping a person from his brothers'
phrases.notes: דברים 24:7

phrases.english: I only know about a man who kidnapped,
from where do we know a woman?
The verse says: 'And one who kidnaps a man.'
phrases.notes: שמות 21:16. Here the kidnapper is just 'one who kidnaps,' so it could be a woman.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא about who counts as kidnapper and victim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman who kidnaps is liable, learned from 'וגונב איש.'

steps.title: What about a woman who kidnaps a woman?
steps.stepSummary: The two פסוקים cover a man kidnapping anyone and a woman kidnapping a man. Where do we learn about a woman kidnapping a woman?
steps.simpleTranslation: So far I know about a man who kidnapped, whether he took a woman or a man, and a woman who kidnapped a man. How do we know about a woman who kidnapped a woman?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא sums up what each פסוק covered and asks about the one case still missing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In דברים the kidnapper is male, but the victim ('נפש') can be anyone. In שמות the kidnapper can be anyone, but the victim is male ('איש'). Neither פסוק covers a female kidnapper with a female victim.

keyTerms.meaning: Whether a woman or a man
Who (a woman) kidnapped

phrases.english: I only know about a man who kidnapped,
whether a woman or a man,
phrases.notes: This describes who he kidnapped.

phrases.english: and a woman who kidnapped a man.
From where do we know a woman who kidnapped a woman?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the first derivation and finds a case still missing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that a woman who kidnaps a woman is liable.

steps.title: 'That kidnapper shall die' means every case
steps.stepSummary: The words 'ומת הגנב ההוא' teach that any kidnapper dies, in every combination.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'Then that kidnapper shall die,' meaning in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers with another phrase from the פסוק in דברים, which includes every kind of kidnapper and victim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The kidnapper' is said with no limits on who kidnapped or who was taken. So it covers the last case too: a woman who kidnaps a woman.

keyTerms.meaning: That kidnapper
In any case; no matter what

steps.whatToRemember: Every combination is liable: a man or a woman who kidnaps a man or a woman.

phrases.english: The verse says:
'Then that kidnapper shall die' —
phrases.notes: דברים 24:7

phrases.english: in any case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of the step before.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'ומת הגנב ההוא' includes every kidnapper, so a woman who kidnaps a woman is liable.

steps.title: Which victims make the kidnapper liable
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא: kidnapping a man, a woman, a convert, a freed slave or a child all make him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'If a man is found kidnapping a person from his brothers.' Whether he kidnaps a man, a woman, a convert, a freed slave or a child, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that lists all the kinds of victims that count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'From his brothers' could make us think only a full-born Jewish adult counts. The ברייתא says a גר, a freed slave and a קטן are also 'brothers' for this law.

keyTerms.meaning: A convert
A freed slave
A child (minor)

phrases.english: Another baraita teaches:
'If a man is found kidnapping a person from his brothers' —
whether one kidnaps a man,
or one kidnaps a woman,
or a convert,
or a freed slave or a child —
he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ברייתא that widens the list of victims.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Kidnapping a man, a woman, a convert, a freed slave or a minor brings liability.

steps.title: No liability without a completed sale
steps.stepSummary: If he kidnapped but did not sell, or sold but the victim is still in his control, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he kidnapped him but did not sell him, or sold him but he is still in his control, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives the conditions for liability. Kidnapping alone is not enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק requires both kidnapping and selling ('ומכרו'). The sale must also be complete, meaning the victim has left the kidnapper's hands.

keyTerms.meaning: He kidnapped him
He sold him
In his control or possession
Exempt

phrases.english: He kidnapped him and did not sell him,
he sold him but he is still in his domain —
phrases.notes: The victim hasn't actually left the kidnapper's hands yet.

phrases.english: he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with the conditions for liability.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liability needs a completed sale that takes the victim out of the kidnapper's control.

steps.title: Selling the victim to his own relatives still counts
steps.stepSummary: If he sold the victim to the victim's father, brother or another relative, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sold him to his father, his brother or one of his relatives, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא teaches that a sale to the victim's own family is still a real sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think selling him back to his family is like returning him. The ברייתא says it is still a sale, so the kidnapper is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Relatives
Liable

steps.confusionAlert: 'His father' and 'his brother' mean the victim's family, not the kidnapper's.

phrases.english: If he sold him to his father or to his brother
or to one of the relatives —
he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a case of sale that still counts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling the victim to the victim's own relatives brings liability.

steps.title: Kidnapping slaves is exempt
steps.stepSummary: One who kidnaps slaves is exempt from the death penalty for kidnapping.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who kidnaps slaves is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by excluding slaves from the list of victims that count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A freed slave counts (step 38), but someone who is still a slave does not. This fits 'from his brothers' in the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Slaves

steps.whatToRemember: For the death penalty for kidnapping: any free Jew counts as a victim, including a גר, a freed slave and a קטן. The victim must be sold and handed over, even if he is sold to his own relatives. A slave does not count.

phrases.english: One who kidnaps slaves is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the ברייתא by excluding slaves.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Kidnapping slaves does not bring the death penalty for kidnapping.
